items.headline: Judge rules FCC violated ABC's free speech rights
items.summary: A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from reviewing all local broadcast licenses held by ABC, whose stations air in six major U.S. markets. The ruling found the FCC's actions violated the network's free speech rights.

items.headline: New U.S. tariffs target China, EU and 12 others
items.summary: The administration plans a new 20% tariff on most Chinese products and additional tariffs of 10% to 20% on other partners, possibly starting in January. It is relying on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 after the Supreme Court ruled against its use of emergency powers in February.

items.headline: Storms snarl Thanksgiving travel; Macy's parade moved to Saturday
items.summary: Strong winds, high tides, heavy rain and flooding are expected to affect travel for an estimated 81.5 million people. NBC said the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed to Saturday because powerful winds were forecast for New York.

items.headline: Army destroys lead azide stockpile in Iowa
items.summary: The Army detonated the nation's entire five-ton stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown after a federal court approved it. FEMA reported no detectable lead in the air, while environmental groups are demanding a full accounting of the effects.

items.headline: FCC clears SpaceX plan for 1 million satellites
items.summary: The FCC approved SpaceX's plan to deploy 1 million satellites to host data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical of the plan.

items.headline: Alaska ends voter-data deal with Justice Department
items.summary: Alaska's Republican elections official ended an agreement that shared state voter registration data with the Justice Department. The department had been searching such data for noncitizens, which could flag voters for possible removal.

items.headline: Support grows for Princeton scientist held by ICE
items.summary: Princeton doctoral candidate Eva Yi Xie, a Chinese national, was detained by ICE on Nov. 19 at Reagan National Airport, and a federal judge has barred her transfer out of Virginia while her petition is pending. About 250 people rallied at Princeton, and New Jersey lawmakers have pressed for her return.

items.headline: Settler violence marks West Bank olive harvest
items.summary: Palestinians in the West Bank are finishing an olive harvest the U.N. calls the most violent on record amid rising settler attacks. Some former Israeli generals have stepped in to help protect Palestinian farmers.

items.headline: Climate change threatens U.S. cranberry harvest
items.summary: Climate change is shifting the narrow growing conditions cranberries need. Scientists and growers are working to protect the crop, most of which the U.S. supplies to the world.

items.headline: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65
items.summary: Andy Taylor, guitarist of the 1980s English band Duran Duran, has died at 65. He had disclosed a stage 4 prostate cancer diagnosis in 2022, and musicians and fans have paid tribute.

digest.overview:
A federal judge ruled the FCC violated ABC's free speech rights and blocked the administration from reviewing the network's local broadcast licenses. The White House announced new tariffs on China, the European Union and 12 other partners, including a 20% rate on most Chinese goods, possibly starting in January. The Army destroyed the nation's five-ton lead azide stockpile in Iowa, and FEMA reported no detectable lead in the air. Storms threaten Thanksgiving travel for an estimated 81.5 million people, and the Macy's parade was moved to Saturday. The FCC approved SpaceX's plan to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. A judge ordered Georgia's Fulton County to give the state election board a copy of 2020 records seized by the FBI, and Alaska ended a voter-data agreement with the Justice Department. The Steelers released Aaron Rodgers.

Abroad, Yemen's Houthis set Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery ablaze and threatened Red Sea ports after the Saudi-led coalition warned of a strike on Hodeida. Gaza's Health Ministry declared an epidemic alert over meningitis as Israeli strikes killed at least 10 people Tuesday. Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian attacks that have hit at least 14 Russian refineries this month. South Korea's central bank raised its key rate to 3.25% and lifted its growth forecasts, while rail workers began a work-to-rule ahead of a planned Dec. 10 strike. Seoul is among the 14 economies in the new U.S. tariff round, which keeps its 15% cap. In the West Bank, former Israeli generals are escorting Palestinians through an olive harvest the U.N. calls the most violent on record.

fact.answer:
Cutting an apple breaks open its cells and lets an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase mix with natural compounds called polyphenols. Once oxygen reaches them, the enzyme oxidizes the polyphenols, and the products react to form brown pigments. Scientists call this enzymatic browning.

The brown pigments belong to the melanin family, the same group that gives human skin its color. Researchers think the reaction helps plants defend against pests and pathogens. The same process also gives prunes, raisins, coffee, black tea and cocoa their dark colors.

To keep slices looking fresh, refrigerate them or coat them with lemon or pineapple juice, whose acids and antioxidants slow the reaction. Pears, bananas, avocados and potatoes brown the same way.

word.definition: To bring things that seem to clash into agreement or harmony, such as two sets of figures, two points of view, or two people after a falling-out; also, to come to accept something unwelcome.
